newsitem.title: USA: Iraq TV shows CIA spies, U.S. disputes claim.
newsitem.headline: Iraq TV shows CIA spies, U.S. disputes claim.

text.p: Iraqi television on Friday showed four Iraqis who confessed to spying for the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency but in Washington officials dismissed Baghdad's claims of having uncovered a CIA spy network.
Saad Daham Awad, 32, an officer in the Iraqi army, appeared on state-run Iraqi television in the evening and in a relaxed manner explained how he was recruited to spy for the CIA.

Awad, wearing civilian clothes, said he was approached by a Kurd in northern Iraq working for the CIA's Iraq Trust group that used as its cover building hospitals in the area. He later recruited his brother Salah, who along with two other Iraqis who confessed to spying also appeared on the programme.
The Kurdish north has been under the control of the Kurds since after the 1991 Gulf War and the region is protected from Iraqi forces by a U.S.-led air operation.
Awad said he started off smuggling medicine from Baghdad to the north and later started turning over information on the Iraqi army.
"Iraqi Intelligence has uncovered a spy and sabotage group which works for the American Central Intelligence Agency," the Iraqi News Agency INA said, quoting state-run television, earlier in the day.
"Baghdad television said members of the group have confessed their activities against Iraq, its people and its leader President Saddam Hussein," INA said.
INA gave no further details on how the group was caught or if it was connected to the recent assassination attempt on the life of President Saddam Hussein's eldest son, Uday.
Uday, who appeared on Iraqi television on Tuesday for the first time since he was shot, appeared to blame neighbouring Iran for the attack.
A CIA spokesman in the United States declined to comment on the report but U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said the charge was nothing more than propaganda.

"Frankly, if anybody believes these reports they ought to have their heads examined. This is a well-noted and tired propaganda ploy," Burns told a news briefing before Awad appeared on Iraqi television.
Iraq's announcement of the spy group comes one week after Uday was attacked by unidentified gunmen while he was driving in the wealthy al-Mansour district of the Iraqi capital.
Another U.S. official suggested the Iraqi report was aimed at showing Saddam's eldest son Uday was in control after surviving an apparent assassination attempt last week.

The official said any Iraqis put on display as alleged CIA agents could include some people detained by Iraqi troops in early September after Iraqi forces drove into the Western-protected Kurdish safe haven in northern Iraq to help one Kurdish faction against a second faction.
Iraqi dissident groups in Europe have said that when the Iraqi troops entered the north, they broke up a long-standing CIA-funded covert operation to destabilise the Iraqi president.
This is not the first time Iraq has accused the United States, which led the allied force that drove Iraq out of Kuwait in 1991, of recruiting agents to carry out acts of sabotage.
Last March Baghdad said the United States had recruited agents who planted car bombs in the capital Baghdad, Tikrit and other Iraqi cities.
In the same month Iraq also accused Gulf War foe Kuwait of recruiting agents who carried out sabotage attacks against the Iraqi people, U.N. observers and arms inspectors.
Iraq's state-run television then interviewed six Iraqis from Basra who said the Kuwaiti secret police had recruited them to plant bombs in various parts of the country.
